findings.claim: All five borough entries carry Heat Vulnerability Index scores, AC-access shares and cooling-centre-density figures in the `value` field, four with a `level` derived from them (Bronx 100, Brooklyn 100, Manhattan 70, Queens 100, Staten Island -20).
findings.whatIFound: R10 violation. The dimension's headline indicator is heat-related mortality; no borough `value` measures it. I checked for genuine borough-level heat mortality before nulling, per instruction. The 2026 DOHMH report page states only that 'age-adjusted death rates were highest in Brooklyn and the Bronx' — for heat-STRESS deaths only — and the page explicitly 'does not provide borough-level mortality rates'; it also publishes no borough heat-exacerbated rate. The NYC Comptroller's 'Overheated, Underserved' (4 Aug 2022), the source cited for four of the five boroughs, likewise 'does not provide borough-level mortality rates'. No borough heat-mortality or heat-stress ED-visit rate was obtainable. So no real borough headline value exists and the proxies were sitting in the promoted field: the build pipeline would have rendered 'the Bronx's heat mortality is HVI 5'.
findings.correction: All five boroughs set to value: null, `level` removed entirely, proxy content moved into `note` and labelled as a proxy naming what it actually measures (HVI = modelled vulnerability composite; cooling-centre density = facility supply; AC access = risk factor). DOHMH's qualitative 'highest in Brooklyn and the Bronx' preserved in those two notes. Result: 0 of 5 boroughs with real data, 5 of 5 with named proxies — the honest encoding per R6.

findings.claim: Black New Yorkers die of heat stress at ~2x the age-adjusted rate of white New Yorkers: 0.8 vs 0.4 deaths per million (2014-2023); Latino New Yorkers at ~1.0 per million.
findings.whatIFound: The 0.8 vs 0.4 (2014-2023) pair is the PRIOR vintage — the 2025 report, which I confirmed at the 2025 archive page. The 2026 report the dossier headlines states verbatim: 'Black and Latino New Yorkers had higher age-adjusted heat-stress death rates compared with white New Yorkers (1.2 and 1.0 deaths per million, respectively, compared with 0.4 deaths per million) from 2016-2025' and 'Black New Yorkers had heat-stress death rates three times higher and Latino New Yorkers had death rates two times higher than white New Yorkers.' So the dossier pairs a 2026 headline with 2025-vintage rates and UNDERSTATES the current disparity as 2:1 when DOHMH now reports 3:1. Aggravating: the dossier's own sourcesFetched entry records having fetched '1.2 vs 0.4' from this exact page and flags it as 'internally inconsistent' — the correct figure was retrieved and then discarded in favour of the stale one. The dossier also mixed vintages within one sentence, giving the Latino rate from the 2026 vintage (1.0) alongside Black/white rates from the 2025 vintage.
findings.correction: Black 1.2, Latino 1.0, white 0.4 age-adjusted heat-stress deaths per million, 2016-2025 (2026 report): Black 3x and Latino 2x the white rate. Prior vintage (2025 report, 2014-2023): Black 0.8 vs white 0.4, 2x. Earliest vintage (2022 report, 2011-2020): Black 2.2 vs white 0.9, 2x.

findings.claim: The Black:white rate ratio is stated in the same `value` field, immediately after the ~500 heat-related deaths/year headline, with nothing marking that they describe different populations.
findings.whatIFound: The reviewer's arithmetic suspicion is confirmed by the source. DOHMH's per-million race rates apply ONLY to direct heat-stress deaths — 1.2 per million against ~8.3M residents is consistent with a single-digit annual count, and matches the 7/yr direct average, not the ~500 total. DOHMH publishes NO race-disaggregated heat-exacerbated death rates: the 2026 report page 'does not provide heat-exacerbated death rates broken down by race or ethnicity', and the equity finding for that ~490/yr component is qualitative in DOHMH's own wording ('inequitably affects Black New Yorkers, reflecting the impacts of structural racism'). The dossier therefore attached a direct-heat-stroke rate ratio to a heat-exacerbated headline covering ~98% of the deaths. This is the dimension's key equity fact and as drafted it was silently describing a different population from the headline.
findings.correction: State explicitly that the 3:1 (2026) / 2:1 (2025) ratio measures DIRECT heat-stress mortality only (~7 deaths/yr), and that no race-disaggregated rate exists for the ~490/yr heat-exacerbated component, where DOHMH's inequity finding is qualitative. Corroborating single-year fact retained: of the 21 heat-stress deaths in 2025, 18 were Black or Latino.

findings.claim: ~500 estimated heat-related deaths/year (2026 report) 'and rising relative to the ~350/year figure cited in earlier report vintages'.
findings.whatIFound: R11 resolved. The 2026 report exists and is dated as claimed: '2026 New York City Heat-Related Mortality Report', released 15 June 2026 (DOHMH press release pr2026). Three vintages, each an annual average over a different pooled window, all confirmed from primary sources: (a) 2022 report, released 16 June 2022 — ~370 deaths/yr; race rates 2011-2020 (Black 2.2 vs white 0.9). (b) 2025 report, released 30 June 2025 — ~525/yr pooled 2018-2022, about 3% of all warm-season deaths, of which ~5/yr heat-stress and ~520/yr heat-exacerbated; race rates 2014-2023 (0.8 vs 0.4). (c) 2026 report — ~500/yr, of which heat-stress avg 7/yr pooled 2016-2025 and heat-exacerbated avg ~490/yr pooled 2014-2023. So the orchestrator's ~350 is the 2022-vintage ~370. The step from ~370 to ~500-525 spans both a moved pooling window and DOHMH's successive refinement of the heat-exacerbated excess-mortality model — it is a methodology and scope shift, not a demonstrated trend. And 'rising' is wrong as stated: the current 500 is BELOW the previous vintage's 525.
findings.correction: Headline ~500/yr from the 2026 report (released 15 June 2026), stated explicitly as a multi-year annual average (heat-stress pooled 2016-2025; heat-exacerbated pooled 2014-2023). Replace 'and rising' with the vintage ladder 370 (2022) -> 525 (2025) -> 500 (2026) and state that the differences are principally pooling-window and model revision.

findings.claim: Global lens level 70, on an adaptation-capacity/climate-finance-equity framing, with the rationale conceding 'NYC's own share of responsibility for this gap is not separately quantified in the sources reviewed'.
findings.whatIFound: Under R2 this is a comparative capacity benchmark, not a quantified transmission channel: it says NYC can self-finance seawalls while Lagos, Dhaka and Manila cannot. That is a fact about NYC's wealth and about global finance architecture; no trade, procurement, finance or waste-export channel connecting NYC to those cities' adaptation shortfall is quantified anywhere in the entry, and the entry says so itself. R2 is explicit that a precise-looking level attached to an unquantified claim 'is a finding, not a result', and that a null with strong framing beats an invented number. It does NOT duplicate the climate-change dimension's global lens — I confirmed that one is scored 120 on consumption-based emissions overshoot per R12, and this entry deliberately avoids emissions attribution — so the division of labour the agent asked about is sound; only the score is not.
findings.correction: Global level set to null; confidence lowered to low; framing retained as honest qualitative content with named parties who could quantify it (NYC Comptroller's Bureau of Climate & Sustainability, UNEP AGR team, loss-and-damage attribution researchers).

findings.claim: UNEP figures cited as 'US$187-359B/year (2024 report) to US$215-387B/year (2023 report)', with '$310B/year by 2035' and '~12x the ~$26-28B/year in actual international public adaptation finance flows (2022-2023)', sourced to the 2024 report with `year: 2024`.
findings.whatIFound: The AGR 2024 range is CONFIRMED: gap US$187-359B/yr; international public adaptation finance flows rose from US$22B (2021) to US$28B (2022); and even meeting the Glasgow doubling goal would close only ~5% of the gap. But the current vintage as of July 2026 is the Adaptation Gap Report 2025, 'Running on Empty' (Nov 2025), which the dossier neither cites nor dates: gap US$284-339B/yr by 2035; needs US$310-365B/yr by 2035 (US$440-520B inflation-adjusted to 2035); international public flows US$26B in 2023; needs 12-14x current flows. The dossier silently blended the two — it took the '$310B by 2035' and the '12x' from the 2025 report while citing only the 2024 report and setting year 2024. The '$215-387B/year (2023 report)' figure I could not verify and have removed. UNEP's own resource page returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so figures are confirmed via Carbon Brief and SEI summaries rather than the primary PDF; confidence capped accordingly.
findings.correction: Headline the AGR 2025 vintage ('Running on Empty', Nov 2025): gap US$284-339B/yr by 2035 against US$26B/yr international public flows in 2023, i.e. needs 12-14x current flows. Carry AGR 2024's US$187-359B/yr as the prior vintage. Drop the unverified US$215-387B figure. Set year to 2025.

findings.claim: Borough notes assign HVI 5 to 'East Tremont' (Bronx), 'the Rockaways' (Queens) and 'East Harlem' (Manhattan), all cited to NYC Comptroller, 'Overheated, Underserved'; and a subIndicator states '12 NTAs citywide score 5'.
findings.whatIFound: The Comptroller report's HVI-5 list is: East Flatbush, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Fordham and University Heights, Highbridge and Concourse, Brownsville, Central Harlem, East New York and Starrett City, Jamaica and Hollis, Hunts Point and Longwood, Morrisania and Crotona, Mott Haven and Melrose — eleven neighbourhoods, five of them in the Bronx. East Tremont, the Rockaways and East Harlem are NOT on it; the Manhattan HVI-5 neighbourhood is CENTRAL Harlem, and the Queens one is Jamaica and Hollis, not the Rockaways. The count is 11, not 12. Everything else the dossier drew from this report is confirmed verbatim: Manhattan 7.1 and Queens 5.0 cooling centres per 100,000; East Flatbush 2 centres for 162,446 residents = 1.2 per 100,000, the most underserved neighbourhood citywide and 85% Black; Bedford-Stuyvesant 9 centres for 174,960 = 5.1 per 100,000; and 'Staten Island has the lowest heat vulnerability of all five boroughs, in part because rates of home ownership are relatively high.' Report date: 4 August 2022.
findings.correction: Replace the three unsupported neighbourhood attributions with the Comptroller's actual list; Manhattan note now names Central Harlem (Comptroller-sourced) and flags East Harlem as unverified against this source; Queens note names Jamaica and Hollis. HVI-5 count corrected to 11 per the Comptroller (2022), with the caveat that HVI vintages and geographies change.

findings.claim: 'Local Law 85 of 2020 / Local Law 128' and 'a 2026 City Council bill pushing a goal of 7 cooling centers per 100,000 residents, with an operating plan due by May 2026'.
findings.whatIFound: Local Law 85 of 2020 is real (public education and communication about cooling centres). The companion is Local Law 128 OF 2025, enacted from Int 0998-2024 and passed by the Council in September 2025 — not an unnumbered statute and not a 2026 bill. It codifies the cooling-centre programme, requires an annual public plan each May, requires NYCEM to designate 'where practicable ... no fewer than 7 cooling centers per 100,000 residents', requires siting to consider the Heat Vulnerability Index and vulnerable populations, and sets the comprehensive cooling and communication plan due on or before 15 May 2026. So the density goal is already law, not a pending 2026 bill — a materially more favourable status than the dossier states, in the city's favour.
findings.correction: Rename the anchor 'Local Law 85 of 2020 / Local Law 128 of 2025' and restate: the 7-per-100,000 target and the May-15-2026 plan deadline are statutory as of September 2025, from Int 0998-2024, not a pending bill.

findings.claim: dataGaps: 'The exact current-year (2023 or later) total citywide GHG emissions figure in MtCO2e could not be confirmed to the ton in this research pass'; and the secondary percent-change figures '-26% since 2006, -2% since 2019, -6% since 2022'.
findings.whatIFound: Settled portrait-wide by ruling R13: the current vintage is CY2024 = 47,944,551 tCO2e, -25.2% vs the 2005 baseline of 64,139,721 and -4.9% vs CY2023's 50,433,720 (published Dec 2025, NYC Open Data wq7q-htne). The dossier's percent-change figures use a 2006 baseline and conflict with the settled series. This dimension makes no claim that requires the inventory total, so the gap is deleted rather than filled.
findings.correction: Remove the GHG data gap and the conflicting percent-change figures. If the figure is ever needed here, use CY2024 = 47,944,551 tCO2e (-25.2% vs 2005) per R13.

findings.claim: Basement Apartment Conversion Pilot Program (Local Law 126) creates 'a legal pathway (min. ceiling heights, egress windows, flood-proofing, ventilation)' and is 'direct policy response to the Hurricane Ida basement-apartment deaths'.
findings.whatIFound: The law number and year are correct — Local Law 126 OF 2024, tied to City of Yes for Housing Opportunity; units must have existed before 20 April 2024; owners must apply via DOB by 20 April 2029; DOB/HPD published proposed rules in 2025 (HPD press release 074-25). But properties in FLOOD-PRONE AREAS ARE NOT ELIGIBLE for the programme. That materially undercuts describing it as the policy response to deaths caused by basement flooding, and 'flood-proofing' is not among its requirements (the listed requirements are smoke and gas alarms, central heating, proper egress, and wall separation from boiler equipment). The programme is a housing-safety and legalisation measure that specifically excludes the highest-flood-risk stock.
findings.correction: Add the flood-prone-area exclusion explicitly, cite Local Law 126 of 2024, remove 'flood-proofing' from the requirement list, and reframe the relevance: it addresses illegal-basement housing safety generally but excludes flood-prone properties, so it does not directly cover the Ida risk pattern.

findings.claim: Citywide home-AC access '91.0% of households have home AC (~9% lack it)'.
findings.whatIFound: Defensible but over-precise. The DOHMH HVI page gives 91%; City Limits, reporting the same 2026 DOHMH report, says 'around 90 percent'. One-decimal precision is not supported by either.
findings.correction: State as '~90-91% of households have home AC (~9-10% lack it)'.

findings.claim: Data gap: floodplain population 'reported inconsistently ... ~400,000 ... ~605,300 ... ~1.3 million' — could not settle on an authoritative number. Dossier states Sandy only qualitatively and Ida as '13 people in one night'.
findings.whatIFound: Settled by extracting the DCP Info Brief PDF that defeated the agent's fetch (text extraction succeeded). NYC Department of City Planning, 'Flood Risk in NYC' Info Brief, November 2016, using FEMA's 2015 PFIRMs: 400,000 residents, 183,000 residential units, 72,000 buildings, 291,000 jobs and 532M sq ft of floor area in the 1% annual chance floodplain — and 'by the 2050s, the number of people living in the 1% annual chance floodplain could more than double.' That is the authoritative in-floodplain figure. The 1.3 million is Rebuild by Design's deliberately broader count of residents 'within or directly adjacent to' the floodplain (all block groups touching it, 2015 PFIRM + 2018 ACS), rising to 2.2M by 2100 under NPCC3 — a different definition, not a conflicting measurement. A ~440,000 'residents affected' figure appears for the 2013/2015 PFIRM expansion, and a ~1.5M figure appears in 2021 Stormwater Resiliency Plan press material. The dossier's '~605,300' I could not source and have removed. Note the base number rests on 2015 PFIRMs that NYC successfully appealed in October 2016 and FEMA agreed to revise, so it is both dated and contested. Sandy: 43 NYC resident deaths and ~$19B in damages (NYC Comptroller, 'Ten Years After Sandy'; the SIRR report 'A Stronger, More Resilient New York' is dedicated to the 43) — the brief's '44' is a common variant and DOHMH counts 52 injury deaths on a broader direct-plus-indirect definition. Ida: 13 NYC deaths reported at the time with 11 in basement apartments; DOHMH's later analysis counts 14 Ida-related injury deaths of which 10 (71%) were drownings in unregulated illegal basement apartments; record 3.15 in of rain in one hour.
findings.correction: Replace the unsettled gap with: 400,000 residents in the 1% annual chance floodplain (DCP Info Brief, Nov 2016, FEMA 2015 PFIRMs), projected to more than double by the 2050s; 1.3M 'in or directly adjacent to' (Rebuild by Design); ~440,000 and ~1.5M variants noted; 605,300 removed as unsourceable. Add verified Sandy (43 deaths, ~$19B) and Ida (13 deaths / 11 in basement apartments, or 14 / 10 illegal on DOHMH's definition; 3.15 in/hr) figures as context.

findings.claim: The dossier never states NPCC sea-level-rise ranges or names the current NPCC assessment, referring to 'NPCC sea-level-rise overlays' only in a data gap and an expert entry.
findings.whatIFound: Gap rather than error, now filled from the primary summary PDF. The latest published assessment is NPCC4, 'New York City Climate Risk Information 2022: Observations & Projections' (published April 2024; Braneon et al., Annals of the NY Academy of Sciences 2024). Projections: sea level +7-11 in in the next decade, +14-19 in by the 2050s, +25-39 in by the 2080s, and up to +65 in by the start of the next century, with a higher worst case that cannot be ruled out; average annual temperature +2.7-3.9°F by the 2030s, +4.0-6.0°F by the 2050s, +5.6-9.8°F by the 2080s; average annual rainfall up to +14% by the 2050s and +22% by the 2080s, with more extreme rainfall events. NPCC5 is underway (co-chairs Sheila Foster, Columbia; Timon McPhearson, The New School) but has not superseded NPCC4. Note the older NPCC (2015) ranges of 8-30 in by the 2050s embedded in the DCP brief have been superseded by NPCC4's narrower 14-19 in.
findings.correction: Added an NPCC4 subIndicator with the SLR, temperature and rainfall ranges, the April 2024 publication date, and a note that NPCC5 is in progress.

findings.claim: Cool Neighborhoods NYC (2017), CoolRoofs, and the HEAP Cooling Assistance Benefit terms ('$800 portable/$1,000 wall-sleeve including installation', '2026 applications closed June 5, 2026', 'cannot have received a HEAP-funded AC in the prior five years').
findings.whatIFound: All confirmed. Cool Neighborhoods NYC launched 2017 as a $106M initiative, of which $82M for tree planting targeted at the South Bronx, Central Brooklyn and Northern Manhattan, plus CoolRoofs, heat-risk training for home health aides, and Be A Buddy NYC. NYC CoolRoofs dates from 2009, recoats up to ~1M sq ft per summer with ~70 workers, and has coated more than 10M sq ft citywide, targeted at the highest-heat-vulnerability districts. HEAP Cooling Assistance: one AC or fan per household, not to exceed $800 with installation for a window/portable unit or fan and not to exceed $1,000 for an existing wall-sleeve unit; the eligibility criterion 'Not have received a HEAP-funded air conditioner within the past five years' is verbatim from ACCESS NYC; the 2025-2026 benefit closed 5 June 2026. The actions themselves are NYC-specific and real; NYC-EJA's Extreme Heat & Air Quality campaign and The Point CDC's Be A Buddy programme both exist. No private individual's contact details appear anywhere in the dossier.

findings.claim: Local Law 41 of 2021 (Climate Resiliency Design Guidelines): 'By 2026 all city capital projects are required to meet the full Climate Resiliency Design Guidelines standard.'
findings.whatIFound: Law number and year correct — Local Law 41 was passed in March 2021, codified at NYC Admin Code § 3-131, and required creation of climate resilience guidelines for capital projects plus a resilience scoring system. By 2026 all city capital projects must meet the guidelines, covering a ~$90B capital portfolio; a pilot ran on 40 projects across 23 agencies. The guidelines exclude coastal protection projects, for which separate guidance is being developed — a scope limit the dossier omits. The agent's own caveat that it could not verify a 2026 compliance-rate report stands.
findings.correction: Add the coastal-protection-project exclusion; keep the unverified-compliance-rate caveat.

findings.claim: '$196.7B FY2025-2035 citywide capital plan'; '$2.7B+ Lower Manhattan Coastal Resiliency'; ESCR 'Phase 1 completed ahead of schedule and under budget ... southern phase ... expected complete by early 2027'; the USACE 'three Actionable Elements' and 'a 30-day state/agency review ... completed May 6, 2026'; and Cloudburst hubs each losing '$46-50M in federal funding'.

levelReview.reasoning: R12 CANNOT BE APPLIED LITERALLY HERE, and the corrected dossier says so instead of quietly substituting a city policy target. This is one of the two locally-defined ecological dimensions under R6: there is no Raworth planetary boundary for urban heat mortality and no DEAL downscaled per-capita benchmark, so 'score against the framework benchmark' has no direct analogue. The benchmark I am scoring against, stated explicitly: ZERO PREVENTABLE HEAT DEATHS. That is the defensible framework-equivalent because DOHMH itself frames these deaths as preventable and the dominant risk factor is a purchasable good — home AC and the ability to run it — not an irreducible meteorological hazard; and unlike a statutory target it applies identically to any city portrait, satisfying R12's actual purpose of cross-portrait comparability. Against that benchmark, 100 holds. Anchoring on the headline: ~500 heat-related deaths/yr, ~3% of all warm-season deaths, heat being NYC's deadliest weather hazard, against a benchmark of zero. R1 adjustments, all upward or neutral: the direct heat-stress racial disparity has WIDENED, not closed, in the current vintage (Black 3x white, up from 2x) nine years after Cool Neighborhoods NYC made closing it an explicit aim; 2025 produced 21 heat-stress deaths, the highest single-year tally in over a decade, 19 of them in one four-day June heat wave and 18 of the 21 Black or Latino; ~493,000 rental households have AC they do not run because of utility cost, meaning ownership statistics overstate real protection; the most heat-vulnerable neighbourhood citywide by HVI, East Flatbush (85% Black), has 1.2 cooling centres per 100,000 against Manhattan's 7.1. Downward pull factors considered and judged insufficient to move the score: citywide AC penetration of ~90-91% is genuinely high (R5 requires reporting that honestly); Local Law 128 of 2025 now makes the 7-per-100,000 cooling-centre target statutory; Local Law 41 of 2021 mandates resilient design across the ~$90B capital portfolio from 2026; CoolRoofs has coated 10M+ sq ft. Those are real and are credited in the rationale, but they are inputs, not outcomes, and the outcome measure has not improved. R5 also names heat-mortality inequity specifically as one of the three genuine crises the portrait must not launder. Not raised to 150 (emergency) because programmes exist and are expanding and the toll is not accelerating on a like-for-like basis. Global lens moved 70 -> null under R2: the adaptation-capacity framing is a comparative capacity benchmark with no quantified NYC transmission channel, and the entry itself conceded NYC's share is unquantified.
levelReview.r12Note: R12 has no literal analogue: locally-defined ecological dimension, no planetary boundary, no DEAL downscaled benchmark. Benchmark used and stated explicitly in levelRationale: zero preventable heat deaths. This is stated rather than assumed, per the review instruction.
